passage:
Sunday.
Mom did The Phone Talk today. I was ready for her to ask for my password. She didn't. She sat on my bed and said, "Here's what I worry about: strangers asking for photos, anyone asking you to keep secrets from us, and you not sleeping. Your chats with friends are yours. I won't read them."
Then we agreed: the phone charges in the kitchen at night, and if anyone online ever makes me uncomfortable, I tell her, and I won't be in trouble for it. Mom (Madhuri to everyone else) says she'll "check in" every Sunday, just asking, not scrolling.
A friend from tuition has parents who read every single message. He's just got better at hiding things. I think Mom's way is smarter. I'd actually tell her stuff.
Ujjwal

qa.q: Where will the phone charge at night?
qa.a: The phone charges in the kitchen at night.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel when Mom started The Phone Talk?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt wary, braced for Mom to ask for the password, and was relieved when she said the chats with friends would stay private.

qa.q: Which parts of Mom's approach build safety and trust together?
qa.a: She named the real risks, said chats with friends are private, set a charging rule, promised no trouble for reporting, and will check in by asking, not scrolling.

qa.q: What does the friend from tuition show about reading every message?
qa.a: It shows that total checking can backfire: that friend has only got better at hiding things.

grounding: A mother explains safety rules openly, agrees what stays private, and checks in on risk without reading every message.

passage:
The day Jeevan got his first phone, his mother Farida sat with him on the verandah of their house in the small town, the fields turning gold behind them.
"Three rules," she said. "One: no strangers, no photos to anyone you don't know. Two: the phone sleeps in the kitchen at night. Three: if anything online ever scares you, you tell me, and you won't be in trouble for telling."
Jeevan nodded, waiting for the fourth rule, the one where she'd read everything.
It didn't come. "Your chats with your friends are yours," she said. "I won't read them. Every Sunday I'll just ask, 'Anything bothering you?' That's all."
He blinked. His friend's father checked every message, and his friend had a second secret phone.
A month later, a stranger sent Jeevan a strange link. He showed his mother that same evening, without even thinking twice.

qa.q: Where does the phone sleep at night?
qa.a: The phone sleeps in the kitchen at night.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when the fourth rule didn't come?
qa.a: Jeevan felt surprised and trusted, since he had expected his mother to read everything.

qa.q: Why did Farida's approach work?
qa.a: Open rules and privacy for his chats made Jeevan feel safe telling her, so he showed her the strange link the same evening.

qa.q: What would change if Farida had read every message?
qa.a: Jeevan might have hidden things better, like his friend with the second secret phone, instead of coming to her.

grounding: It shows a parent explaining safety rules openly, agreeing what is private and checking in on risk, leading her teen to report a stranger.

passage:
In their small apartment in Singapore, Wei's father Noa sat across the dinner table with a sheet of paper.
"You're fourteen. You want the social media account. Let's agree how it'll work."
Wei braced for the worst.
Noa wrote as they talked. The account stays private. No sharing their address or school. Location off. "And I won't read your messages. That's your space. But if someone asks you to keep a secret from us, or makes you uncomfortable, you tell me, and you won't lose the account for it."
Wei looked at the paper. "That's it?"
"That's it. Every Friday I'll ask how it's going. You can say 'fine.'"
Two months later, a stranger who claimed to be a talent scout asked Wei to video-chat alone and not tell anyone. Wei walked into the kitchen that night and showed his father. Noa said, "Thank you for telling me," and they blocked and reported the account together.

qa.q: Where do Wei and Noa live?
qa.a: In their small apartment in Singapore.

qa.q: How did Wei feel before Noa explained the rules?
qa.a: Wei felt tense and braced for the worst, expecting strict surveillance.

qa.q: Which part of Noa's approach helped when the stranger appeared?
qa.a: Promising that Wei wouldn't lose the account for telling made it safe to report the stranger, so they blocked and reported it together.

qa.q: How does Noa see his role as a parent here?
qa.a: Noa sees his role as setting open safety rules and checking in, not reading every message, trusting Wei to come to him.

grounding: It shows a parent agreeing open safety rules and private space with a teen, which leads the teen to report a risky contact.

passage:
The school counsellor's room was small, and Gurleen sat as far from her father as the two chairs allowed.
"She hid a whole friendship from us for months," her father said. "So I started checking her phone every night."
"And after that?" asked Rehana, the counsellor.
"She deleted everything before I checked."
Rehana turned to Gurleen. "Why did you hide the friendship?"
Gurleen's voice was small. "Because last time, Papa read my chats aloud at dinner and laughed."
Her father looked down.
Rehana drew three boxes on a sheet. "Safety rules, which you both agree on. Private things, which Papa doesn't read. And a weekly check-in, where Gurleen can say if anything feels risky." She looked at Gurleen's father. "Watching everything often teaches teenagers to hide better, not to be safer."
Her father took the pen slowly. "Can we try the boxes?" Gurleen nodded, and her shoulders dropped a little.

qa.q: How many boxes did Rehana draw on the sheet?
qa.a: Rehana drew three boxes on a sheet.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling when she explained why she hid the friendship?
qa.a: Gurleen felt hurt and embarrassed, remembering Papa reading her chats aloud and laughing, which made the truth feel unsafe.

qa.q: What did Rehana suggest to balance safety and trust?
qa.a: Rehana suggested agreed safety rules, a private space Papa doesn't read, and a weekly check-in about anything risky.

qa.q: How does Gurleen's father seem to feel after hearing her reason?
qa.a: Her father seems ashamed and ready to change, looking down and then asking to try the boxes.

grounding: A counsellor helps a parent move from reading every message to open safety rules, agreed privacy and check-ins, after surveillance made his daughter hide more.

passage:
Dear Kashish,
Now that you have your own phone, I wanted to write this down instead of making it a lecture at dinner.
Here's what I promise: I won't read your chats with your friends. Your messages, your jokes, your crushes: those are yours. I remember being fourteen.
Here's what I'll ask: the phone charges in the kitchen at night. Location sharing stays on when you go out. And if anyone online asks you to keep a secret from us, or to meet, or for photos, you tell me, and you won't be in trouble for it. Ever.
Once a week, on Sunday, let's just talk: anything weird, anything you liked, anything that worried you.
I know Bhavna aunty checks every message on Dev's phone. I'm not going to, because I'd rather you tell me things than learn to hide them better.
Love,
Mumma

qa.q: Where will the phone charge at night?
qa.a: The phone charges in the kitchen at night.

qa.q: Why does Mumma choose not to read Kashish's chats?
qa.a: Mumma would rather be trusted than spy, hoping Kashish will come to her instead of learning to hide things better.

qa.q: Which parts of the letter balance safety and privacy?
qa.a: Clear safety rules like charging in the kitchen and location sharing, a promise not to read chats, a no-trouble rule for secrecy or meeting requests, and Sunday talks.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Kashish might feel respected and relieved that the chats stay private, and safer knowing anything weird can be reported without trouble.

grounding: Shows a parent explaining safety rules openly, agreeing what stays private and checking in on risk without reading every message.
